claim: Optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes decreases behavioral mechanosensitivity.
source: We show that optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes decreases behavioral and cellular mechanosensitivity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes decreases cellular mechanosensitivity.
source: We show that optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes decreases behavioral and cellular mechanosensitivity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Keratinocyte-mediated mechanosensitivity processes are inherently mediated by ATP signaling.
source: These processes are inherently mediated by ATP signaling, as demonstrated by complementary cutaneous ATP release and degradation experiments.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on ATP release and degradation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Specific deletion of P2X4 receptors in sensory neurons markedly decreases behavioral mechanical sensitivity.
source: Specific deletion of P2X4 receptors in sensory neurons markedly decreases behavioral and primary afferent mechanical sensitivity, thus positioning keratinocyte-released ATP to sensory neuron P2X4 signaling as a critical component of baseline mammalian tactile sensation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on genetic knockout experiments.

claim: Specific deletion of P2X4 receptors in sensory neurons markedly decreases primary afferent mechanical sensitivity.
source: Specific deletion of P2X4 receptors in sensory neurons markedly decreases behavioral and primary afferent mechanical sensitivity, thus positioning keratinocyte-released ATP to sensory neuron P2X4 signaling as a critical component of baseline mammalian tactile sensation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on genetic knockout experiments.

claim: Keratinocyte-released ATP to sensory neuron P2X4 signaling is a critical component of baseline mammalian tactile sensation.
source: Specific deletion of P2X4 receptors in sensory neurons markedly decreases behavioral and primary afferent mechanical sensitivity, thus positioning keratinocyte-released ATP to sensory neuron P2X4 signaling as a critical component of baseline mammalian tactile sensation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion based on the combined findings from ATP release and P2X4 knockout experiments.

claim: Merkel cells constitute only 3-6% of total skin cells.
source: Notably, Merkel cells constitute only a small portion (3–6%) of total skin cells (Moll et al., 1986; Fradette et al., 2003; Halata et al., 2003), whereas keratinocytes, which have traditionally been known for their roles in barrier formation and protection rather than sensory transduction, comprise 94–97% of the epidermis (Fuchs, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Keratinocytes comprise 94-97% of the epidermis.
source: Notably, Merkel cells constitute only a small portion (3–6%) of total skin cells (Moll et al., 1986; Fradette et al., 2003; Halata et al., 2003), whereas keratinocytes, which have traditionally been known for their roles in barrier formation and protection rather than sensory transduction, comprise 94–97% of the epidermis (Fuchs, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Keratinocytes are closely apposed to sensory nerve terminals.
source: However, keratinocytes are closely apposed to sensory nerve terminals (Löken et al., 2009) and are constantly exposed to external mechanical forces in the environment like brushing and pressure from stimuli like clothing, objects and other living organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Isolated keratinocytes directly respond to mechanical probing by increasing intracellular calcium concentrations.
source: Previously, it was demonstrated that isolated keratinocytes directly respond to mechanical probing by increasing intracellular calcium concentrations (Koizumi et al., 2004; Tsutsumi et al., 2009; Goto et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Keratinocytes can release ATP, calcitonin gene-related peptide β (CGRPβ), acetylcholine, glutamate, epinephrine, neurotrophic growth factors, and cytokines.
source: Furthermore, keratinocytes can release many neuroactive substances including ATP, calcitonin gene-related peptide β (CGRPβ), acetylcholine, glutamate, epinephrine, neurotrophic growth factors, and cytokines among others (Barr et al., 2013; Hou et al., 2011; Lumpkin and Caterina, 2007; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of keratinocytes evokes inward currents in adjacent sensory neurons in co-cultures.
source: In co-cultures of keratinocytes and dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons, mechanical stimulation of keratinocytes evokes inward currents in adjacent sensory neurons, presumably through release of one of the aforementioned metabolites (Klusch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of keratinocytes causes membrane depolarization in a stimulus-dependent manner.
source: Increasing indentation revealed a stimulus-dependent depolarization that returned to baseline between each stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GFP expression overlaps substantially with K14-positive epidermal cells in Arch-K14Cre+ skin.
source: As expected, GFP (Figure 1C,F) overlapped substantially with K14-positive epidermal cells (Figure 1B,E) in Arch-K14Cre+ skin (Figure 1G), but not in Arch-K14Cre- skin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Arch-K14Cre+ keratinocytes exhibit hyperpolarized membrane potentials during 590 nm light stimulation.
source: During light stimulation, Arch-K14Cre+ keratinocytes exhibited hyperpolarized membrane potentials, as compared to no light stimulation (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: 590 nm light stimulation has no effect on the membrane potential of Arch-K14Cre- keratinocytes.
source: Light stimulation had no effect on the membrane potential of keratinocytes from Arch-K14Cre- animals (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: 590 nm light significantly reduces the overall level of depolarization in Arch-K14Cre+ keratinocytes during mechanical stimulation at each force.
source: Analogous to Figure 1A, the membrane voltage of Arch-K14Cre+ keratinocytes depolarized in a graded manner upon mechanical stimulation, and 590 nm light significantly reduced the overall level of depolarization at each force (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Keratinocyte inhibition significantly elevated mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds in Arch-K14Cre+ animals compared to Arch-K14Cre- controls.
source: Keratinocyte inhibition significantly elevated mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds in Arch-K14Cre+ animals compared to Arch-K14Cre- controls (Figure 1J), reflecting decreased tactile sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: 590 nm light caused Arch-K14Cre+ animals to be less responsive to repeated suprathreshold probing than their Arch-K14Cre- littermates.
source: The 590 nm light caused Arch-K14Cre+ animals to be less responsive to repeated probing than their Arch-K14Cre- littermates (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: 490 nm light had no effect on the mechanical responsiveness of Arch-K14Cre+ or Arch-K14Cre- animals.
source: Control light (490 nm) had no effect on the mechanical responsiveness of the Arch-K14Cre+ or Arch-K14Cre- animals (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Arch-K14Cre+ animals exposed to 590 nm light exhibited significantly fewer noxious and innocuous responses to needle poke compared to Arch-K14Cre- controls.
source: Arch-K14Cre+ animals exposed to 590 nm light exhibited significantly fewer noxious and innocuous responses, and a concomitant increase in null responses to the needle poke compared to Arch-K14Cre-controls (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Arch-K14Cre+ animals exposed to 590 nm light exhibited a concomitant increase in null responses to needle poke compared to Arch-K14Cre- controls.
source: Arch-K14Cre+ animals exposed to 590 nm light exhibited significantly fewer noxious and innocuous responses, and a concomitant increase in null responses to the needle poke compared to Arch-K14Cre-controls (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Neither 590 nm nor 490 nm light altered the temperature in the hindpaw skin.
source: Importantly, the behavioral changes observed in response to the 590 nm light were not a result of temperature changes in the hindpaw skin as neither 590 nm nor 490 nm light altered the temperature in the hindpaw skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Neither Arch-K14Cre+ nor Arch-K14Cre- animals preferred either chamber when the lights were on in the place preference assay.
source: Neither Arch-K14Cre+ nor Arch-K14Cre- animals preferred either chamber when the lights were on (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the inhibition of keratinocytes and other epidermal cells alone does not evoke aversive or pleasant sensations in the animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Inhibition of keratinocytes and other epidermal cells alone does not evoke aversive or pleasant sensations in the animals.
source: Neither Arch-K14Cre+ nor Arch-K14Cre- animals preferred either chamber when the lights were on (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the inhibition of keratinocytes and other epidermal cells alone does not evoke aversive or pleasant sensations in the animals.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the place preference data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Epidermal K14-expressing cells play a key role in detecting evoked innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that epidermal K14-expressing cells play a key role in detecting evoked innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: ChR expression is present throughout the keratinocyte layers in ChR-K14Cre+ animals.
source: Similar to the pattern of expression of Arch in Arch-K14Cre+ sections, ChR expression was present (Figure 2E) throughout the keratinocyte layers, extensively overlapping with K14 immunoreactivity (Figure 2D) in ChR-K14Cre+ animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: All keratinocytes from ChR-K14Cre+ animals responded with a sustained inward current during 490 nm light stimulation.
source: All keratinocytes from ChR-K14Cre+ animals responded with a sustained inward current during a 30 second 490 nm light stimulation (Figure 2G–I), whereas none of the ChR-K14Cre- keratinocytes responded (Figure 2I); only a small leak current was present in some cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: None of the ChR-K14Cre- keratinocytes responded to 490 nm light stimulation.
source: All keratinocytes from ChR-K14Cre+ animals responded with a sustained inward current during a 30 second 490 nm light stimulation (Figure 2G–I), whereas none of the ChR-K14Cre- keratinocytes responded (Figure 2I); only a small leak current was present in some cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: ChR-K14Cre+ animals responded to hindpaw light stimulation within 46 seconds on average.
source: On average, ChR-K14Cre+ animals responded to hindpaw light stimulation within 46 seconds, whereas most ChR-K14Cre- controls did not respond to the 473 nm laser stimulation during the 6 min test (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Most ChR-K14Cre- controls did not respond to 473 nm laser stimulation during the 6 min test.
source: On average, ChR-K14Cre+ animals responded to hindpaw light stimulation within 46 seconds, whereas most ChR-K14Cre- controls did not respond to the 473 nm laser stimulation during the 6 min test (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The majority of mice from either genotype did not respond to the 589 nm control laser.
source: The majority of mice from either genotype did not respond to the 589 nm control laser (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ChR-K14Cre+ animals spent significantly more time attending to their 473 nm light-stimulated hindpaw than ChR-K14Cre- littermates.
source: Additionally, ChR-K14Cre+ animals spent significantly more time attending to their 473 nm light-stimulated hindpaw (Figure 2—video 1) than ChR-K14Cre- littermates (Figure 2—video 2); most of the ChR-K14Cre- mice were unresponsive to the stimulus for the 6 min duration of the test (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No difference was noted in skin temperature during light stimulation between ChR-K14Cre+ and ChR-K14Cre- genotypes.
source: Once again, these results could not be accounted for by increases in skin temperature, as no difference was noted in skin temperature during light stimulation between genotypes and because either the 473 nm or 589 nm laser elicited the same small temperature increase in both genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Light-induced depolarization of K14-expressing cells elicits attending responses in vivo.
source: These data indicate that light-induced depolarization of K14-expressing cells elicits attending responses in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ChR activation experiments.

claim: ChR-K14Cre- and ChR-K14Cre+ animals spent the same amount of time on the 595 nm and 460 nm-paired sides during light on and light off conditions.
source: ChR-K14Cre- and ChR-K14Cre+ animals spent the same amount of time on the 595 nm and 460 nm-paired sides during light on and light off conditions (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by place preference data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The 460 nm light evoked significantly more 'grooming' and attending behaviors in the ChR-K14Cre+ than in their littermate controls.
source: Upon closer inspection of the animal behaviors on the two sides, it became apparent that the 460 nm light evoked significantly more 'grooming' and attending behaviors in the ChR-K14Cre+ than in their littermate controls (Figure 2L).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Keratinocyte signaling is necessary for naive behavioral responses to both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli.
source: Taken together, these data make clear that keratinocyte signaling is necessary for naive behavioral responses to both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli, and that activation of keratinocytes and other epidermal cells alone is sufficient to elicit behavioral responses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined optogenetic inhibition and activation experiments.

claim: Activation of keratinocytes and other epidermal cells alone is sufficient to elicit behavioral responses.
source: Taken together, these data make clear that keratinocyte signaling is necessary for naive behavioral responses to both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli, and that activation of keratinocytes and other epidermal cells alone is sufficient to elicit behavioral responses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined optogenetic inhibition and activation experiments.

claim: Primary keratinocytes from adult glabrous skin depolarize upon mechanical stimulation in an indentation-dependent manner.
source: However, we show here that primary keratinocytes from adult glabrous skin do depolarize upon mechanical stimulation in an indentation-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Arch inhibition during focal mechanical stimulation of keratinocytes significantly reduced the overall level of depolarization at each indentation.
source: Moreover, Arch inhibition during focal mechanical stimulation of keratinocytes significantly reduced the overall level of depolarization at each indentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ChR activation directly elicits inward currents in P2X2 expressing HEK-293 cells.
source: Conversely, we show that ChR activation directly elicits inward currents in P2X2 expressing HEK-293 cells, thereby showing that the depolarization of keratinocytes is sufficient to release ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Depolarization of keratinocytes is sufficient to release ATP.
source: Conversely, we show that ChR activation directly elicits inward currents in P2X2 expressing HEK-293 cells, thereby showing that the depolarization of keratinocytes is sufficient to release ATP.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the ChR cell sniff assay data.

claim: Transient ATP release was detected during all of the epidermal stimulations.
source: The skin was then probed with forces ranging from 1.6 to 84.8 mN. Transient ATP release was detected during all of the epidermal stimulations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP biosensor data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Increasing mechanical forces applied to glabrous skin resulted in graded, increased ATP release.
source: To determine whether ATP release was graded according to stimulus intensity, increasing mechanical forces were applied to the glabrous skin with von Frey filaments. Increasing forces resulted in graded, increased ATP release (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP biosensor data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Repeated stimulation with a single force (20.1 mN) elicited reproducible ATP release.
source: Further, repeated stimulation with a single force (20.1 mN) elicited reproducible ATP release (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP biosensor data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ATP is released in a reproducible and graded manner by mechanical stimulation of isolated glabrous hindpaw skin.
source: These data indicate that ATP is released in a reproducible and graded manner by mechanical stimulation of isolated glabrous hindpaw skin.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ATP biosensor experiments.

claim: P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells showed robust inward currents when a nearby keratinocyte was mechanically stimulated.
source: P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells, but not GFP- cells, showed robust inward currents when a nearby keratinocyte was mechanically stimulated as shown in current trace examples (Figure 3G) and current density (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: GFP- HEK-293 cells did not show robust inward currents when a nearby keratinocyte was mechanically stimulated.
source: P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells, but not GFP- cells, showed robust inward currents when a nearby keratinocyte was mechanically stimulated as shown in current trace examples (Figure 3G) and current density (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: The magnitude of evoked current in GFP+ HEK cells increased with increasing indentation of the nearby keratinocyte.
source: Further, the magnitude of evoked current in GFP+ HEK cells increased with increasing indentation of the nearby keratinocyte (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Keratinocytes from naive adult mouse skin are capable of rapidly releasing ATP in response to mechanical probing.
source: These results demonstrate that keratinocytes from naive adult mouse skin are capable of rapidly releasing ATP in response to mechanical probing and that the amount of ATP released is indentation-dependent.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cell sniff assay experiments.

claim: The amount of ATP released from keratinocytes is indentation-dependent.
source: These results demonstrate that keratinocytes from naive adult mouse skin are capable of rapidly releasing ATP in response to mechanical probing and that the amount of ATP released is indentation-dependent.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cell sniff assay experiments.

claim: Exposure to 590 nm light blunted the amplitude of the mechanically evoked currents in P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells co-cultured with Arch-K14-Cre+ keratinocytes.
source: Keratinocytes were mechanically stimulated in the presence or absence of 590 nm light, and inward currents in the P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells were recorded. Exposure to the 590 nm light blunted the amplitude of the mechanically evoked currents in the sniffer cells compared to the light off current amplitudes (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: 490 nm light-induced depolarization of ChR-K14Cre+ keratinocytes was sufficient to elicit inward currents in P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells in an intensity-dependent manner.
source: Light-induced 490 nm depolarization was sufficient to elicit inward currents in an intensity-dependent manner, whereas no depolarization occurred with 590 nm light (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: 590 nm light did not elicit depolarization in P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells co-cultured with ChR-K14Cre+ keratinocytes.
source: Light-induced 490 nm depolarization was sufficient to elicit inward currents in an intensity-dependent manner, whereas no depolarization occurred with 590 nm light (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: ATP release from keratinocytes is largely voltage-dependent.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that ATP release from keratinocytes is largely voltage-dependent and that its release is amenable to optogenetic manipulations
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the optogenetic cell sniff assay experiments.

claim: ATP release from keratinocytes is amenable to optogenetic manipulations.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that ATP release from keratinocytes is largely voltage-dependent and that its release is amenable to optogenetic manipulations
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the optogenetic cell sniff assay experiments.

claim: Apyrase injection significantly elevated paw withdrawal thresholds compared with vehicle-injected animals.
source: Apyrase injection significantly elevated paw withdrawal thresholds compared with vehicle-injected animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Apyrase-treated animals responded significantly fewer times to repeated suprathreshold stimulation than vehicle-treated animals.
source: Apyrase-treated animals also responded significantly fewer times to repeated suprathreshold stimulation than vehicle-treated animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Apyrase-injected animals showed a significant decrease in both the number of noxious and innocuous responses to needle stimulation and a concomitant increase in the number of null responses.
source: Further, Apyrase-injected animals showed a significant decrease in both the number of noxious and innocuous responses to needle stimulation and a concomitant increase in the number of null responses (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Acute hydrolysis of ATP in hindpaw skin reduces the responsiveness to both noxious and innocuous mechanical stimuli under baseline conditions.
source: Therefore, acute hydrolysis of ATP in hindpaw skin reduces the responsiveness to both noxious and innocuous mechanical stimuli under baseline conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the apyrase behavioral experiments.

claim: Apyrase attenuated the inward currents in P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells when added to the extracellular buffer while nearby keratinocytes were mechanically stimulated.
source: Importantly, investigation of apyrase at the cellular level through utilizing the cell sniff assay demonstrated that the apyrase used in this study does indeed degrade ATP, as the inward currents in P2X2-GFP+ HEK-293 cells were attenuated when apyrase was added to the extracellular buffer while nearby keratinocytes were mechanically stimulated evoked (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Apyrase treatment overall significantly decreased the action potential firing rate of C-fibers.
source: C-fiber action potentials in response to a force ramp of 20, 40, 75 and 110 mN over a 12 second period were recorded. Apyrase treatment overall significantly decreased the action potential firing rate of the C-fibers (##p=0.0051), two-way ANOVA, Sidak post-hoc test (n = 22 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Apyrase treatment overall decreased action potential firing over the different forces as compared to PBS treatment in the Aδ-Fibers.
source: Apyrase treatment overall decreased action potential firing over the different forces as compared to PBS treatment in the Aδ-Fibers (####p<0.0001), and at the 150 mN force, apyrase action potential firing was significantly decreased as compared to PBS (**p=0.0017), two-way ANOVA, Sidak post-hoc test.
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There was a significant decrease in action potential firing in the SA-Aβ-fibers treated with apyrase as compared to those incubated with PBS.
source: There was a significant decrease in action potential firing in the SA-Aβ-fibers treated with apyrase as compared to those incubated with PBS (##p=0.0025), two-way ANOVA, Sidak post -hoc test.
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds of C-fibers as evaluated by von Frey filaments.
source: Apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds as evaluated by von Frey filaments (PBS: 5.88 ± 5.88 mN, apyrase: 5.88 ± 5.88 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.60) or conduction velocity (PBS: 0.55 ± 0.22 m/s, apyrase: 0.53 ± 0.24 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.79) of C-fibers.
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Apyrase had no effect on the conduction velocity of C-fibers.
source: Apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds as evaluated by von Frey filaments (PBS: 5.88 ± 5.88 mN, apyrase: 5.88 ± 5.88 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.60) or conduction velocity (PBS: 0.55 ± 0.22 m/s, apyrase: 0.53 ± 0.24 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.79) of C-fibers.

evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds of Aβ-fibers as measured by von Frey filaments.
source: Like C-fibers, apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds of Aδ-fibers (PBS: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN, apyrase: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.70) or Aβ-fibers (PBS: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN, apyrase: 4.00 ± 5.19 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.80) as measured by von Frey filaments, or the conduction velocities of Aδ-fibers (PBS: 7.28 ± 0.47 m/s, apyrase: 6.60 ± 0.55 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.36) or Aβ-fibers (PBS: 17.71 ± 2.87 m/s, apyrase: 14.31 ± 0.81 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.25).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Apyrase had no effect on the conduction velocities of Aδ-fibers.
source: Like C-fibers, apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds of Aδ-fibers (PBS: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN, apyrase: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.70) or Aβ-fibers (PBS: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN, apyrase: 4.00 ± 5.19 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.80) as measured by von Frey filaments, or the conduction velocities of Aδ-fibers (PBS: 7.28 ± 0.47 m/s, apyrase: 6.60 ± 0.55 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.36) or Aβ-fibers (PBS: 17.71 ± 2.87 m/s, apyrase: 14.31 ± 0.81 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.25).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Apyrase had no effect on the conduction velocities of Aβ-fibers.
source: Like C-fibers, apyrase had no effect on the mechanical thresholds of Aδ-fibers (PBS: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN, apyrase: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.70) or Aβ-fibers (PBS: 4.00 ± 2.82 mN, apyrase: 4.00 ± 5.19 mN; median ± interquartile range; Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.80) as measured by von Frey filaments, or the conduction velocities of Aδ-fibers (PBS: 7.28 ± 0.47 m/s, apyrase: 6.60 ± 0.55 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.36) or Aβ-fibers (PBS: 17.71 ± 2.87 m/s, apyrase: 14.31 ± 0.81 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test, p=0.25).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Apyrase treatment did not alter the rheobase values of DRG neurons as compared to the PBS control.
source: Apyrase treatment did not alter the rheobase (current required to elicit one action potential) values as compared to the PBS control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Apyrase treatment did not alter the resting membrane potential of DRG neurons.
source: In addition, apyrase treatment did not alter the resting membrane potential of the neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cutaneous ATP signaling is essential for normal behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that cutaneous ATP signaling is essential for normal behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli and is required at cutaneous terminals for afferent firing elicited by mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the apyrase experiments.

claim: Cutaneous ATP signaling is required at cutaneous terminals for afferent firing elicited by mechanical stimuli.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that cutaneous ATP signaling is essential for normal behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli and is required at cutaneous terminals for afferent firing elicited by mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the apyrase experiments.

claim: The combined apyrase treatment and 590 nm light inhibition of K14-expressing epidermal cells had no additive effect on behavioral mechanical thresholds when compared to vehicle with 590 nm light.
source: The combined apyrase treatment and 590 nm light inhibition of K14-expressing epidermal cells had no additive effect on behavioral mechanical thresholds (Figure 5A), or on responses to repeated suprathreshold stimulation (Figure 5B) when compared to vehicle with 590 nm light.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The combined apyrase treatment and 590 nm light inhibition of K14-expressing epidermal cells had no additive effect on responses to repeated suprathreshold stimulation when compared to vehicle with 590 nm light.
source: The combined apyrase treatment and 590 nm light inhibition of K14-expressing epidermal cells had no additive effect on behavioral mechanical thresholds (Figure 5A), or on responses to repeated suprathreshold stimulation (Figure 5B) when compared to vehicle with 590 nm light.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: K14-expressing cells are the major source of ATP in skin.
source: This suggests that K14-expressing cells are the major source of ATP in skin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of additive effect of apyrase and optogenetic inhibition.

claim: The effects of apyrase treatment were not significantly different from that of both optogenetic inhibition and apyrase treatment in the noxious needle assay.
source: In the noxious needle assay, the effects of apyrase treatment were not significantly different from that of both optogenetic inhibition and apyrase treatment, again suggesting that K14-expressing cells are a major source of the ATP that is required for noxious mechanosensation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Other non-K14-expressing cells are not a significant source of mechanically evoked ATP release in skin.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that other non-K14-expressing cells are not a significant source of mechanically evoked ATP release in skin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of additive effect of apyrase and optogenetic inhibition.

claim: ATP is the major signaling molecule released from keratinocytes in response to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimulation of normal skin.
source: Furthermore, because there was no additive effect of apyrase together with optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes, the data make clear that ATP is the major signaling molecule released from keratinocytes in response to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimulation of normal skin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of additive effect of apyrase and optogenetic inhibition.

claim: Apyrase-treated ChR-K14Cre+ animals exhibited their first response to the 473 nm light significantly later than the ChR-K14Cre+ animals treated with PBS.
source: Apyrase-treated ChR-K14Cre+ animals exhibited their first response to the 473 nm light significantly later than the ChR-K14Cre+ animals treated with PBS (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Light-induced activation of keratinocytes is sufficient to evoke attending behavioral responses.
source: These data indicate that light-induced activation of keratinocytes is sufficient to evoke attending behavioral responses and that ATP release from skin is an essential signaling molecule involved in these attending responses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ChR activation and apyrase experiments.

claim: ATP release from skin is an essential signaling molecule involved in attending responses.
source: These data indicate that light-induced activation of keratinocytes is sufficient to evoke attending behavioral responses and that ATP release from skin is an essential signaling molecule involved in these attending responses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ChR activation and apyrase experiments.

claim: ATP is a major signaling molecule released from keratinocytes especially in response to mechanical stimulation.
source: Taken together, these results show that ATP is a major signaling molecule released from keratinocytes especially in response to mechanical stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined optogenetic and apyrase experiments.

claim: 5-BDBD significantly increased the mechanical thresholds in naive animals.
source: 5-BDBD significantly increased the mechanical thresholds in naive animals (Figure 6A) and significantly decreased the responsiveness to repeated mechanical probing compared to vehicle (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 5-BDBD significantly decreased the responsiveness to repeated mechanical probing compared to vehicle.
source: 5-BDBD significantly increased the mechanical thresholds in naive animals (Figure 6A) and significantly decreased the responsiveness to repeated mechanical probing compared to vehicle (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Neither low nor high concentration of NF 110 affected baseline mechanical sensitivity as measured in the Up-Down mechanical threshold assay.
source: Neither concentration affected baseline mechanical sensitivity as measured in either the Up-Down mechanical threshold or in the suprathreshold assay, in these mice 60 min after subcutaneous injection (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Neither low nor high concentration of NF 110 affected baseline mechanical sensitivity as measured in the suprathreshold assay.
source: Neither concentration affected baseline mechanical sensitivity as measured in either the Up-Down mechanical threshold or in the suprathreshold assay, in these mice 60 min after subcutaneous injection (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mechanically induced release of ATP from keratinocytes is most likely acting through P2X4 receptors.
source: These data demonstrate that mechanically induced release of ATP from keratinocytes is most likely acting through P2X4 receptors.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the pharmacological experiments with 5-BDBD and NF 110.

claim: Subcutaneous ivermectin administration significantly decreased mechanical withdrawal thresholds.
source: Subcutaneous ivermectin administration significantly decreased mechanical withdrawal thresholds (Figure 6E) and significantly increased responsivity to repeated suprathreshold stimulation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Subcutaneous ivermectin administration significantly increased responsivity to repeated suprathreshold stimulation.
source: Subcutaneous ivermectin administration significantly decreased mechanical withdrawal thresholds (Figure 6E) and significantly increased responsivity to repeated suprathreshold stimulation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Pretreatment with the P2X4 inhibitor 5-BDBD prevented the ivermectin-induced mechanical sensitization in both the mechanical threshold and repeated force assays.
source: Pretreatment with the P2X4 inhibitor 5-BDBD prevented the ivermectin-induced mechanical sensitization in both the mechanical threshold (Figure 6E) and repeated force assays (Figure 6F), indicating that the effects of ivermectin were due to P2X4 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: The effects of ivermectin were due to P2X4 activation.
source: Pretreatment with the P2X4 inhibitor 5-BDBD prevented the ivermectin-induced mechanical sensitization in both the mechanical threshold (Figure 6E) and repeated force assays (Figure 6F), indicating that the effects of ivermectin were due to P2X4 activation.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the 5-BDBD and ivermectin experiments.

claim: Neither 5-BDBD nor ivermectin altered the rheobase of sensory neurons compared to their vehicle controls.
source: Once again, these behavioral results could not be accounted for by altered membrane excitability of sensory neurons due to high concentrations of 5-BDBD or ivermectin as neither drug altered the rheobase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and C) or resting membrane potential of sensory neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D) compared to their vehicle controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Neither 5-BDBD nor ivermectin altered the resting membrane potential of sensory neurons compared to their vehicle controls.
source: Once again, these behavioral results could not be accounted for by altered membrane excitability of sensory neurons due to high concentrations of 5-BDBD or ivermectin as neither drug altered the rheobase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and C) or resting membrane potential of sensory neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D) compared to their vehicle controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in P2rx4 mRNA in lumbar DRG of P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
source: To confirm that P2rx4 is decreased in DRG, we performed qRT-PCR on whole DRG homogenates. As expected, there was a significant decrease in P2rx4 mRNA in lumbar DRG of P2X4-AdvCre+ animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: P2X4 sensory neuron mutants (P2X4-AdvCre+) displayed significantly higher paw withdrawal thresholds when compared with control littermates.
source: P2X4 sensory neuron mutants (P2X4-AdvCre+) displayed significantly higher paw withdrawal thresholds (Figure 7A) and significantly fewer responses to repeated mechanical probing when compared with control littermates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: P2X4 sensory neuron mutants (P2X4-AdvCre+) displayed significantly fewer responses to repeated mechanical probing when compared with control littermates.
source: P2X4 sensory neuron mutants (P2X4-AdvCre+) displayed significantly higher paw withdrawal thresholds (Figure 7A) and significantly fewer responses to repeated mechanical probing when compared with control littermates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: P2X4-AdvCre+ animals had significantly fewer noxious and innocuous responses and more null responses during the noxious needle assay than littermate controls.
source: P2X4-AdvCre+ animals were also less responsive to noxious mechanical stimulation. These animals had significantly fewer noxious and innocuous responses and more null responses during the noxious needle assay than littermate controls (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Ivermectin injection had no effect on mechanical withdrawal thresholds in P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
source: Furthermore, ivermectin injection had no effect on mechanical withdrawal thresholds (Figure 7D) or responsiveness to repeated suprathreshold stimulation (Figure 7E) in P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Ivermectin injection had no effect on responsiveness to repeated suprathreshold stimulation in P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
source: Furthermore, ivermectin injection had no effect on mechanical withdrawal thresholds (Figure 7D) or responsiveness to repeated suprathreshold stimulation (Figure 7E) in P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Apyrase treatment significantly elevated the paw withdrawal threshold of P2X4 AdvCre- animals.
source: Apyrase treatment significantly elevated the paw withdrawal threshold of P2X4 AdvCre- animals (****p<0.0001), but it had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+animals (n.s. p=0.6573), two-way ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Apyrase treatment had no additional effect on paw withdrawal threshold in P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
source: Apyrase treatment significantly elevated the paw withdrawal threshold of P2X4 AdvCre- animals (****p<0.0001), but it had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+animals (n.s. p=0.6573), two-way ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Apyrase treatment significantly lowered the number of responses to the 3.61 mN filament in P2X4-AdvCre- animals.
source: Apyrase treatment significantly lowered the number of responses to the 3.61 mN filament in P2X4-AdvCre- animals (****p<0.0001), but it had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+ animals (n.s. p=0.9126). Furthermore, P2X4-AdvCre- apyrase treated animals were not significantly different from P2X4-AdvCre+ apyrase treated animals (n.s. p=0.4330), two-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Apyrase treatment had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+ animals in the suprathreshold assay.
source: Apyrase treatment significantly lowered the number of responses to the 3.61 mN filament in P2X4-AdvCre- animals (****p<0.0001), but it had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+ animals (n.s. p=0.9126). Furthermore, P2X4-AdvCre- apyrase treated animals were not significantly different from P2X4-AdvCre+ apyrase treated animals (n.s. p=0.4330), two-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Apyrase treatment in P2X4-AdvCre- animals significantly elevated the null responses and decreased both the innocuous and noxious responses in the noxious needle assay.
source: Apyrase treatment in P2X4-AdvCre- animals significantly elevated the null responses (****p<0.0001) and decreased both the innocuous (****p<0.0001) and noxious (****p<0.0001) responses as compared to P2X4-AdvCre- animals treated with PBS. Apyrase treatment had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+ animals compared to the PBS treatment (innocuous n.s. p>0.9999; noxious n.s. p=0.9993; null n.s. p=0.9543), three-way ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Apyrase treatment had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+ animals compared to the PBS treatment in the noxious needle assay.
source: Apyrase treatment in P2X4-AdvCre- animals significantly elevated the null responses (****p<0.0001) and decreased both the innocuous (****p<0.0001) and noxious (****p<0.0001) responses as compared to P2X4-AdvCre- animals treated with PBS. Apyrase treatment had no additional effect on P2X4-AdvCre+ animals compared to the PBS treatment (innocuous n.s. p>0.9999; noxious n.s. p=0.9993; null n.s. p=0.9543), three-way ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Either pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of P2X4 channels specifically from sensory nerve terminals is sufficient to fully decrease the baseline mechanical sensitivity to both innocuous and noxious force.
source: In conclusion, these data demonstrate that either pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of P2X4 channels specifically from sensory nerve terminals is sufficient to fully decrease the baseline mechanical sensitivity to both innocuous and noxious force.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined pharmacological and genetic experiments.

claim: C-fibers from P2X4-AdvCre+ animals had overall significantly reduced firing rates as compared to P2X4-AdvCre- controls.
source: Single nerve recordings from the ex vivo tibial nerve preparation revealed that C-fibers from P2X4-AdvCre+ animals had overall significantly reduced firing rates as compared to P2X4-AdvCre- controls (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The action potential firing rate of slowly adapting myelinated Aδ and Aβ-fibers in response to increasing mechanical stimuli was decreased overall in P2X4-AdvCre+ animals.
source: Furthermore, the action potential firing rate of slowly adapting myelinated Aδ and Aβ-fibers in response to increasing mechanical stimuli was also decreased overall (Figure 8C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data shown in Figure 8C and E.

claim: C-fiber, Aδ-fiber and Aβ-fibers from P2X4-AdvCre+ animals had significantly higher action potential thresholds than their wild type littermates.
source: Remarkably, C-fiber, Aδ-fiber and Aβ-fibers from P2X4-AdvCre+ animals had significantly higher action potential thresholds than their wild type littermates (Figure 8G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data shown in Figure 8G-I.

claim: P2X4 on sensory neuron terminals participates in setting the threshold for mechanical firing of multiple classes of cutaneous sensory neurons.
source: These data indicate that P2X4 on sensory neuron terminals participates in setting the threshold for mechanical firing of multiple classes of cutaneous sensory neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the skin nerve recording data in P2X4 mutants.

claim: Conduction velocities were not altered by the knockdown of P2X4 in C-fibers.
source: Conduction velocities were not altered by the knockdown of P2X4 in any fiber type; C-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 0.72 ± 0.28 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 0.76 ± 0.27 m/s mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test p=0.565), Aδ-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 3.64 ± 1.91 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 3.88 ± 2.29 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test p=0.661) or Aβ-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 12.87 ± 2.67 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 12.76 ± 2.98 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-tests, p=0.913).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Conduction velocities were not altered by the knockdown of P2X4 in Aδ-fibers.
source: Conduction velocities were not altered by the knockdown of P2X4 in any fiber type; C-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 0.72 ± 0.28 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 0.76 ± 0.27 m/s mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test p=0.565), Aδ-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 3.64 ± 1.91 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 3.88 ± 2.29 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test p=0.661) or Aβ-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 12.87 ± 2.67 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 12.76 ± 2.98 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-tests, p=0.913).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Conduction velocities were not altered by the knockdown of P2X4 in Aβ-fibers.
source: Conduction velocities were not altered by the knockdown of P2X4 in any fiber type; C-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 0.72 ± 0.28 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 0.76 ± 0.27 m/s mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test p=0.565), Aδ-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 3.64 ± 1.91 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 3.88 ± 2.29 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-test p=0.661) or Aβ-fibers (P2X4-AdvCre-: 12.87 ± 2.67 m/s, P2X4-AdvCre+: 12.76 ± 2.98 m/s; mean ± SEM; unpaired t-tests, p=0.913).
evidence: This claim is supported by skin nerve recording data.

claim: Sensory neuron-expressed P2X4 is essential for setting both the threshold for initiating mechanical firing and for regulating the firing frequency to suprathreshold sustained stimuli in several classes of slowly adapting sensory neurons in the skin.
source: Together, these data identify sensory neuron P2X4 as a key target of the ATP released from keratinocytes in response to both noxious and innocuous touch and show that sensory neuron-expressed P2X4 is essential for setting both the threshold for initiating mechanical firing and for regulating the firing frequency to suprathreshold sustained stimuli in several classes of slowly adapting sensory neurons in the skin.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined skin nerve recording data in P2X4 mutants.

claim: Sensory neuron P2X4 is a key target of the ATP released from keratinocytes in response to both noxious and innocuous touch.
source: Together, these data identify sensory neuron P2X4 as a key target of the ATP released from keratinocytes in response to both noxious and innocuous touch and show that sensory neuron-expressed P2X4 is essential for setting both the threshold for initiating mechanical firing and for regulating the firing frequency to suprathreshold sustained stimuli in several classes of slowly adapting sensory neurons in the skin.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Keratinocytes communicate with sensory nerve terminals via ATP release, which then activates P2X4 receptors on sensory neurons to signal both innocuous and painful touch perception from the skin.
source: Mechanistically, keratinocytes communicate with sensory nerve terminals via ATP release, which then activates P2X4 receptors on sensory neurons to signal both innocuous and painful touch perception from the skin (Figure 9).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Epidermal Merkel cells' responsiveness to mechanical stimuli and subsequent signaling to sensory neurons are essential for two-point touch discrimination.
source: This concept has recently been challenged by data that demonstrate epidermal Merkel cells' responsiveness to mechanical stimuli and subsequent signaling to sensory neurons, two processes that are essential for two-point touch discrimination (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Keratinocytes have traditionally been known for their roles in barrier formation and protection rather than sensory transduction.
source: Notably, Merkel cells constitute only a small portion (3–6%) of total skin cells (Moll et al., 1986; Fradette et al., 2003; Halata et al., 2003), whereas keratinocytes, which have traditionally been known for their roles in barrier formation and protection rather than sensory transduction, comprise 94–97% of the epidermis (Fuchs, 1995).
evidence: This claim reflects established scientific knowledge about keratinocytes.

claim: Keratinocytes are constantly exposed to external mechanical forces in the environment like brushing and pressure from stimuli like clothing, objects and other living organisms.
source: However, keratinocytes are closely apposed to sensory nerve terminals (Löken et al., 2009) and are constantly exposed to external mechanical forces in the environment like brushing and pressure from stimuli like clothing, objects and other living organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about the location and function of keratinocytes.

claim: Sensory neurons may not be the sole transducers of mechanical stimuli, but rather may collaborate with other cell types such as keratinocytes to initiate or amplify somatosensory signals to sensory neurons.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that sensory neurons may not be the sole transducers of mechanical stimuli, but rather may collaborate with other cell types such as keratinocytes to initiate or amplify somatosensory signals to sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the cited literature.

claim: Purinergic signaling is a critical component of innocuous and noxious skin mechanotransduction, specifically in the context of non-neuronal to neuronal cellular communication.
source: These data are the first to identify purinergic signaling as a critical component of innocuous and noxious skin mechanotransduction, specifically in the context of non-neuronal to neuronal cellular communication.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: Keratin14 is expressed in all keratinocytes as early as E9.5.
source: Keratin14 (K14) is expressed in all keratinocytes as early as E9.5 (Byrne et al., 1994; Dassule et al., 2000; Wang et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Archaerhodopsin-3 pumps protons out of the membrane when activated by amber light, thereby hyperpolarizing the cell.
source: When Arch is activated by amber light (peak photocurrent between 550 and 600 nm), it pumps protons out of the membrane, thereby hyperpolarizing the cell (Chow et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GFP expression was found throughout all keratinocyte layers in Arch-K14Cre+ skin because keratinocytes migrate from the basal to superficial epidermal layers in a temporal fashion.
source: Because keratinocytes migrate from the basal to superficial epidermal layers in a temporal fashion, GFP expression was found throughout all layers, and was not restricted only to the basal keratinocyte layer where K14 expression is found.
evidence: This explanation is based on known biology of keratinocyte migration.

claim: Light pretreatment was not necessary to induce the behavioral mechanical inhibition in Arch-K14Cre+ animals.
source: Although light pretreatments were given for 1 min before application of evoked stimuli for ease of stimuli administration, light pretreatment was not necessary to induce the behavioral mechanical inhibition, as 590 nm light treatment delivered simultaneously with the mechanical stimuli elicited the full effect of inhibition that was observed with pretreatment (compare Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B to Figure 1J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Channelrhodopsin 2 depolarizes cells when activated by 450-500 nm light.
source: Since light-induced inhibition of epidermal cells reduced the animals' baseline sensitivity to evoked mechanical stimuli, we performed complementary experiments to determine the effects of light-induced activation of K14-expressing epidermal cells using light-sensitive Channelrhodopsin 2 (ChR), which depolarizes cells when activated by 450 – 500 nm light (Nagel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ChR is expressed and functional in adult mouse keratinocytes.
source: These data indicate that ChR is expressed and functional in adult mouse keratinocytes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the patch clamp data on ChR-K14Cre+ keratinocytes.

claim: The discrepancies in behavioral responses between the focal hindpaw stimulation and place-preference assay are due to different light power intensities and consequently, different levels of keratinocyte depolarization.
source: Since the same set of epidermal cells are activated by 460 nm light in both assays, we believe the discrepancies in these two behavioral assays are due to different light power intensities and consequently, different levels of keratinocyte depolarization (75.2 μW LED floor in the place preference assay vs. 25 mW laser in the hindpaw light-evoked assay, a 333-fold difference in light intensity).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the behavioral differences.

claim: P2X2 expressing HEK-293 cells exhibit intensity-dependent increases in inward currents in response to light stimulation of ChR-expressing keratinocytes.
source: This hypothesis is further supported by findings in our ChR cell sniff assay where P2X2 expressing HEK-293 cells exhibit intensity-dependent increases in inward currents in response to light stimulation of ChR-expressing keratinocytes, indicating an intensity-dependent release of ATP by keratinocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell sniff assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Keratinocytes possess the functional ion channels required for producing rapid changes in membrane excitability.
source: Other reports using keratinocyte cell lines show that keratinocytes can depolarize or hyperpolarize in response to changes in extracellular ionic gradients (Wohlrab et al., 2000), exhibit increased intracellular Ca2+ in response to mechanical stimuli (Koizumi et al., 2004; Tsutsumi et al., 2009; Goto et al., 2010), and express voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, as well as Transient Receptor Potential channels (Denda et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2008; Caterina and Pang, 2016). These prior reports suggest that keratinocytes possess the functional ion channels required for producing rapid changes in membrane excitability, and our new data reveal that naive adult mouse keratinocytes depolarize in response to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from citations to previous literature.

claim: Keratinocytes likely communicate with sensory nerve terminals via a chemical signaling pathway based on evidence of synapse-like structures between keratinocytes and sensory nerve terminals.
source: This process likely occurs via a chemical signaling pathway based on evidence of synapse-like structures between keratinocytes and sensory nerve terminals (Hilliges et al., 1995; Chateau and Misery, 2004; Château et al., 2007; Klusch et al., 2013; Roggenkamp et al., 2013) and the fact that keratinocytes have been shown to contain and release a variety of neurotransmitter molecules (Burrell et al., 2005; Lumpkin and Caterina, 2007; Barr et al., 2013; Hou et al., 2011Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This hypothesis is based on citations to previous literature.

claim: Graded ATP signaling is essential for the transmission of mechanically relevant information between keratinocytes and sensory neurons.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that graded ATP signaling is essential for the transmission of mechanically relevant information between keratinocytes and sensory neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ATP release and degradation experiments.

claim: It is unlikely that ATP stores from platelets, fibroblasts and neurons are critical for mechanotransduction.
source: While platelets, fibroblasts and neurons also release ATP and are present in the skin (Fukami and Salganicoff, 1977; Grierson and Meldolesi, 1995; Lazarowski et al., 2003; Abbracchio et al., 2009), it is unlikely that ATP stores from these cells are critical for mechanotransduction since in vivo apyrase treatment did not amplify the effects of specific optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of additive effect of apyrase and optogenetic inhibition.

claim: The release of ATP from keratinocytes in response to mechanical stimuli is largely voltage-dependent, thereby pointing towards a vesicular release mechanism for ATP.
source: Additionally, our findings in the Archaerhodopsin cell sniff assay coupled with the data showing that keratinocytes depolarize in an indentation-dependent manner in response to mechanical stimulation, argue that the release of ATP from keratinocytes in response to mechanical stimuli is largely voltage-dependent, thereby, pointing towards a vesicular release mechanism for ATP.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the optogenetic cell sniff assay and patch clamp data.

claim: ATP can be released from keratinocytes via a calcium-dependent vesicular mechanism and/or non-vesicular mechanism via connexin hemichannels.
source: Other studies utilizing normal human epidermal keratinocytes suggest that that ATP can be released via a calcium-dependent vesicular mechanism and/or non-vesicular mechanism via connexin hemichannels (Harden and Lazarowski, 1999; Lazarowski et al., 2003; Inoue et al., 2014; Barr et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The levels of ATP measured in the biosensor experiments are likely underestimations given that both keratinocytes and sensory neurons express ectonucleotidases.
source: Our studies estimate the amount of ATP release to be in the micromolar range, which is an amount sufficient to activate most P2X receptors (Jacobson et al., 2002); however, the levels of ATP we measured are likely underestimations given that both keratinocytes and sensory neurons express ectonucleotidases (Lazarowski et al., 2000; Zylka et al., 2008; Sowa et al., 2010a; Sowa et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is an inference based on known expression of ectonucleotidases.

claim: It is possible that ATP is focally released in high concentration pocket 'domains' between the sensory neuron and keratinocyte cell membranes.
source: Additionally, it is possible that ATP is focally released in high concentration pocket 'domains' between the sensory neuron and keratinocyte cell membranes, and therefore, the ATP concentrations that occur in those localized signaling regions might be much higher than the generalized levels we measured in our assays.
evidence: This is a speculation about the spatial distribution of ATP release.

claim: P2X4 is the most highly expressed P2X receptor on sensory neurons.
source: Although there are a number of P2X channels that have been shown to be expressed by sensory neurons (Kobayashi et al., 2005), we chose to investigate P2X4 because it is the most highly expressed P2X receptor on sensory neurons and because of its relatively equal expression on both light touch and nociceptive neurons (Kobayashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: P2X4 has relatively equal expression on both light touch and nociceptive neurons.
source: Although there are a number of P2X channels that have been shown to be expressed by sensory neurons (Kobayashi et al., 2005), we chose to investigate P2X4 because it is the most highly expressed P2X receptor on sensory neurons and because of its relatively equal expression on both light touch and nociceptive neurons (Kobayashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ATP signaling occurs mainly through P2X4 receptors on sensory neurons.
source: Furthermore, in vivo degradation of ATP had no additional behavioral effect in sensory neuron-specific P2X4 knockout mice, therefore indicating that ATP signaling occurs mainly through P2X4 receptors on sensory neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of additive effect of apyrase in P2X4 mutants.

claim: Purinergic signaling appears to be more multifaceted than would be expected by simply determining the probability of ATP binding via EC50 values.
source: However, purinergic signaling appears to be more multifaceted than would be expected by simply determining the probability of ATP binding via EC50 values because (1) receptors can also exist in heteromeric confirmations and (2) P2 receptors have been shown to have complex response patterns, where rather than having distinct individual roles, different P2 receptors have been shown to work in concert through having both additive and inhibitory interactions (Xing et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents a general principle about purinergic signaling.

claim: Sensory neurons are intrinsically capable of sensing mechanical stimuli via the activation of mechanosensitive ion channels found on their terminals.
source: Sensory neurons are intrinsically capable of sensing mechanical stimuli via the activation of mechanosensitive ion channels found on their terminals.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Piezo2 and Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are key mechanosensitive ion channels found on sensory neurons.
source: Studies have identified Piezo2 and Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) as key mechanosensitive ion channels found on sensory neurons (Coste et al., 2010; Kwan et al., 2009); Vilceanu and Stucky, 2010); Woo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATP is likely a potentiator, rather than an initiator, of action potential firing in response to mechanical stimulation of the skin.
source: ATP is likely a potentiator, rather than an initiator, of action potential firing in response to mechanical stimulation of the skin because we observed blunting of behavioral and afferent mechanical responses and decreased sensitivity thresholds in the various assays instead of finding a complete lack of responsiveness to force.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that responses were reduced but not eliminated.

claim: After skin injury or disease, it is possible that one or more factors in addition to ATP potentiates signals after injury.
source: However, after skin injury or disease, it is possible that one or more of these factors potentiates signals after injury in addition to ATP.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms in disease states.

claim: Injury-induced augmentation of keratinocyte communication could provide sensory neurons with numerous opportunities for initiation and amplification of signaling mechanisms that underlie pain, itch or dysesthesia in the setting of disease.
source: If true, this injury-induced augmentation of keratinocyte communication could provide sensory neurons with numerous opportunities for initiation and amplification of signaling mechanisms that underlie pain, itch or dysesthesia in the setting of disease.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential implications for disease states.

claim: The lesser effect of apyrase in the teased fiber experiments compared to the genetic P2X4 mutant model is most likely due to the apyrase enzyme not being able to penetrate and fully distribute within the tissue to the receptive terminals of sensory neurons.
source: We believe that the lesser effect in the apyrase experiment is most likely due to the apyrase enzyme, which is diluted in aqueous buffer, not being able to penetrate and fully distribute within the tissue to the receptive terminals of sensory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference in results between apyrase and genetic experiments.

claim: Keratinocytes are not only communicating with the more superficial non-peptidergic C-fibers, but also signaling to the deeper-projecting peptidergic C-fibers, Aδ-fiber nociceptors and slowly adapting Aβ-fibers that mediate light touch.
source: These data indicate that keratinocytes are not only communicating with the more superficial non-peptidergic C-fibers (i.e. MrgD+/IB4- binding C-fibers), but also signaling to the deeper-projecting peptidergic C-fibers, Aδ-fiber nociceptors and slowly adapting Aβ-fibers that mediate light touch, all of which are closer to the dermal-epidermal border in the skin (Zylka et al., 2005; Basbaum et al., 2009; Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Le Pichon and Chesler, 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the skin nerve recording data showing effects on all fiber types.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of K14-expressing cells activated slowly adapting Aδ and Aβ-fibers as well as C-fibers.
source: These data are supported by previous studies, which also showed that optogenetic stimulation of K14-expressing cells activated slowly adapting Aδ and Aβ-fibers (Baumbauer et al., 2015) as well as C-fibers (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Pang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Keratinocyte signaling is essential in potentiating signals of many fiber subtypes and that keratinocyte-sensory neuron communication is not a fiber-type-specific phenomenon.
source: Consequently, these data together indicate that keratinocyte signaling is essential in potentiating signals of many fiber subtypes and that keratinocyte-sensory neuron communication is not a fiber-type-specific phenomenon.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that all fiber types tested were affected.

claim: The new custom-designed feedback-controlled mechanical stimulator probe may stimulate the receptive field more evenly and consistently than the von Frey filament tip.
source: The most parsimonious reason for this novel difference is that instead of using von Frey filaments as we have always done in the past, we utilized a new custom-designed feedback-controlled mechanical stimulator probe to exert a continuous force ramp from 0 to 100 mN perpendicularly to each fiber's skin receptive field. The surface area of the new stimulator probe utilized to exert this force is flat, circular and larger (0.8 mm diameter; approximately 2–4 times larger) than the tip of a typical von Frey filament which is small and pointed (4 mN: 0.19 mm diameter; 6 mN: 0.25 mm diameter). Thus, the new probe used for the ramp may stimulate the receptive field more evenly and consistently than the von Frey filament tip which may have sharper edges that deliver more punctate stimuli to the receptive field and activate the fiber at lower thresholds.
evidence: This is an inference to explain why threshold differences were observed with the new stimulator.

claim: Cutaneous sensory terminals are finely tuned to detect and encode the edges of objects touched.
source: This idea is generally supported by previous evidence that cutaneous sensory terminals are finely tuned to detect and encode the edges of objects touched (Wheat and Goodwin, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Diseases such as complex regional pain syndrome and post-herpetic neuralgia are accompanied by increased epidermal ATP release which can lead to excessive activation of P2X receptors on sensory neurons.
source: It has been shown that diseases such as complex regional pain syndrome and post-herpetic neuralgia are accompanied by increased epidermal ATP release which can lead to excessive activation of P2X receptors on sensory neurons (Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Many skin disorders, such as dermatitis and psoriasis, are characterized by altered keratinocyte function and signaling, and also share cutaneous pain as a common debilitating symptom.
source: Many other skin disorders, such as dermatitis and psoriasis, are characterized by altered keratinocyte function and signaling, and also share cutaneous pain as a common debilitating symptom that leads to severely decreased quality of life in affected patients (Man, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.
